Note::TexAccessor::unescape¶

Back to Note TeX Accessor API Reference

Signature¶

Note Note::TexAccessor::unescape() const

Reverse escape()’s Ten-Character Table¶

unescape() returns a new Note, same shape as the input, with every TeX-escaped special-character sequence from escape’s table replaced by the literal character it stands for. It is the exact inverse of escape(): applying the two in sequence, in either order on already plain or already escaped text respectively, is a lossless round trip.

The ten replacements, in the order applied:

Input

Output

\textbackslash{}

\

\{

{

\}

}

\#

#

\$

$

\%

%

\&

&

\_

_

\^{}

^

\~{}

~

Each replacement is a literal substring match, not a general TeX-command unescape: a command that merely resembles one of these — \%something with extra trailing text, for instance — still has its recognized \% prefix replaced, since the match only requires that exact sequence to appear, not that it stand alone. Every other byte is copied unchanged, so text with none of the ten sequences is returned as-is.

The operation is shape-preserving, cell-independent, and returns a fresh Note. Undefined input remains undefined; Bool, Int64, Float64, and Bytes receivers are rejected because TeX source is Text.

Example 1: All Ten Sequences¶

std::cout << pluss::make_note(
    {R"(a\_b \$x\$ 50\% cost \#1 \& more \{y\} \~{} \^{} \textbackslash{})",
     "nothing special here"})
    .tex().unescape()
    << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
["a_b $x$ 50% cost #1 & more {y} ~ ^ \\", "nothing special here"]

Every escaped sequence in the first cell reverts to its literal character; the second cell, with none of the ten sequences, passes through unchanged.

Example 2: A Lossless Round Trip Through escape()¶

const auto original = pluss::make_note({"a_b $x$ 50% cost #1 & more {y} ~ ^ \\"});
const auto round_trip = original.tex().escape().tex().unescape();
std::cout << std::boolalpha << (round_trip == original).all().bool_item() << '\n';

Output¶

true

escape() then unescape() reproduces the exact original text.

Example 3: Undefined And Non-Text Input¶

std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << pluss::Note::undefined().tex().unescape().defined() << '\n';
try {
  (void)pluss::note::make(std::vector<std::int64_t>{1, 2}).tex().unescape();
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "unescape Int64: rejected\n";
}

Output¶

false
unescape Int64: rejected

See Also¶

  • escape: the exact inverse — protect literal text for TeX.

  • to_text: a broader, lossy reduction from authored TeX to plain text — unlike unescape(), it also strips commands and comments.
